notes: American oak, especially new, gives bolder, less subtle oak flavors than French oak.
White Zinfandel, a semi-sweet blush wine, outsells red Zinfandel six to one.
American Grüner Veltliner tends to be medium bodied and lightly fruity, with high acidity and spice.
Reliable warmth gives very ripe fruit and a fruit-forward style rather than an earthy or mineral one.
California Chardonnay is often buttery and full bodied, from malolactic fermentation and oak.
California Pinot Noir is generally more intense and fruity than Burgundy or Oregon.
Zinfandel is powerful and fruity, with high acidity and jammy flavor.
Cabernet Sauvignon ripens fully, giving fruity, full bodied wines often above 14% alcohol.
Alexander Valley wines are known for a rich, fleshy, voluptuous feel from the warm climate.
Its Cabernet Sauvignon often shows chocolate notes and a warm mouthfeel.
Its Chardonnay is rich, with tropical fruit.
Merlot here tends to show plum, tea leaf and black cherry.
Warmer, sunnier patches give the spicy, berry notes of its Zinfandels.
Hot days give color and big berry fruit, while cool nights keep acidity, structure and power.
Columbia Valley wines are very fruit-forward, like California's, but keep some of the balance and structure of European wine.
Warm days and cool nights keep acid and sugar in balance, and the long season lets tannins mature.
Warm Dry Creek Valley is known for juicy Zinfandel with bright fruit, balanced acidity and notes of blackberry, anise and pepper.
Styles range from high-alcohol to balanced and spicy.
Merlot here tends to show plum, tea leaf and black cherry.
Lodi Zinfandels are known as juicy and approachable.
Carneros Pinot Noir is known for crisp acidity, tight structure and spicy berry fruit.
Older clones give lighter, more elegant wines with earthy notes, while newer French clones give more alcohol, concentration and black fruit.
Cool marine air from San Pablo Bay shapes the style, and long seasons bring intense, vivid flavors.
The warm inland part of the county makes full bodied, very ripe reds from Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Petite Sirah and Zinfandel.
Redwood Valley is known for peppery, spicy Zinfandel.
Monterey Chardonnay is associated with mango and guava.
In the late 20th century its Cabernet Sauvignon was known for very vegetal, green pepper flavors.
Mount Veeder wines are typically powerful in structure.
Its Cabernet Sauvignon commonly shows briary flavors, moderate to bold tannin and herbal, floral aromas.
Thin, poor soils give small berries with intense flavor, in wines that need years of aging.
Napa is known above all for Cabernet Sauvignon, with strong black fruit flavors.
Napa Chardonnay is often associated with pineapple notes.
Napa Zinfandel is plummy and intense, with red berry, cedar and vanilla, often in a claret style.
Oakville is known for Bordeaux varieties, with rich texture, firm tannin and notes of mint and herbs.
Its Merlot tends to show ripe blackberry and black raspberry.
Burgundy-style wines dominate Oregon.
Oregon Pinot Gris is medium bodied, yellow to copper-pink, with aromas of pear, apple and melon.
With hot days and cool sea-air evenings, Paso Robles makes Zinfandel known for being soft and round.
The cool climate gives higher acidity and better balance than the fatter, creamier style of the Alexander Valley.
Classic Russian River Pinot Noir has pale but vibrant color, lively acidity and cherry and berry fruit, though newer methods give heavier, fuller wines.
Merlot has a distinctive tea-like note, and Zinfandel shows tarter red fruit than in warmer Dry Creek Valley.
Its crisp grapes are prized for sparkling wine.
Rutherford Merlot tends to show ripe blackberry and black raspberry.
Cooler growing seasons than the surrounding regions give higher acidity in the wines.
Sonoma is known for fruity, ripe Zinfandel.
Sonoma Cabernet tends toward anise and black olive notes.
Alexander Valley Cabernet is known for chocolate notes and a warm mouthfeel.
Warmth, steady breezes and volcanic soil give fruit with concentrated color and intense flavor.
Washington wines are known for bright fruit flavors and crisp acidity.
Recent reds lean riper and more fruit-forward, with noticeable tannin, oak and moderately high alcohol.
Cabernet and Merlot are often lush, with concentrated berry flavors such as blackberry, cherry and raspberry.
Good examples can usually age at least eight years.
Cabernet Franc is fruit-forward, with blueberry and raspberry.
Young Sangiovese plantings here have given spicy, tart cherry wines with anise, red currant and tobacco leaf.
New York Riesling generally has a light body and a light, mellow flavor.
Fog, wind and the Pacific keep days cool here, so the grapes keep plenty of acidity.
Pinot Noir and Chardonnay lead, with a good share of Syrah.
Its Pinot Noir has darker cherry fruit, balanced by savory notes such as earthy spice and tea.
Chardonnay is lean, with bright acidity, green apple and chalk in the west, and fuller, with yellow apple, in the east.
Even at its eastern edge, Sta. Rita Hills is a very cool Winkler Region I.
Pinot Noir, about 65% of the vines, shows bright red cherry, ripe and often with a maraschino accent.
Chardonnay leans toward lemon, green apple or yellow apple, and in some sites toward mineral notes.
Its Syrah is often lean, with whole-cluster spice.
The Santa Ynez Valley warms from Winkler Region I near the coast to Region III in the east.
Chardonnay is the most planted grape, and Pinot Noir is also important.
The warmer east suits Rhône and Bordeaux grapes.
Ballard Canyon calls itself Syrah territory, and more than half its vines are Syrah.
Strong winds, fog and big swings between day and night temper its heat.
Its Syrah has savory notes like the northern Rhône, with riper fruit, fuller body and softer, more plentiful tannins.
Happy Canyon is the warm side of Santa Barbara County, with little fog.
Wind, altitude and day-night swings of up to 50°F give wines a cooler personality than you might expect.
Cabernet Sauvignon can be ripe without being jammy, or show savory herb and mineral notes.
Sauvignon Blanc ranges from ripe tropical and stone fruit to tart citrus, grass and pepper.
Los Olivos District is moderately warm, a cool Winkler Region III, with little fog.
Most vines are Bordeaux and Rhône grapes, and Italian and Spanish grapes are common too.
Winds through the San Antonio River Valley cool Alisos Canyon, but it is warmer and less foggy than its neighbors.
Key grapes in the wider Los Alamos Valley include Chardonnay, Riesling, Pinot Noir, Syrah, Rhône whites and Bordeaux reds.
A long, cool growing season near the Pacific gives ripe flavor while the grapes keep their natural acidity.
Pinot Noir and Chardonnay lead.
Wines across the San Luis Obispo Coast share an energetic acidity and vibrancy.

The Santa Cruz Mountains ripen Cabernet and Syrah into elegant wines, alongside Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
Long built on Pinot Noir, the region is now best known for Cabernet and Cabernet-based wines.
